paragraphs: Friend, here's what this passage teaches me. Bildad says a lot of true-sounding things, like "Does God pervert justice? Does the Almighty pervert what is right?" (Job 8:3). God is just, and that part is solid. But Bildad takes it one step further and says that suffering must mean sin, and that is a step the text never lets us take for him.

Look at how he talks to Job. He brings up Job's children with a cold line about rebellion (Job 8:4), then hands Job a pile of ifs: if you seek God, if you are pure and upright (Job 8:5-6). I think that lands like a bill when Job needed a hug. And did you catch that Bildad calls Job's words "a blustering wind" (Job 8:2), right after Job poured out his heart? A friend can quote good theology and still miss the hurting person standing right in front of him.

So here's what I'd carry out of my bakery today, baker. Before you hand anybody a neat answer for their pain, sit with them first, because a true sentence said coldly can still sting. And when your own hard season comes, don't let a tidy formula talk you into believing you know why. Bildad ends his speech, but the conversation isn't over, and neither is the story of Job, so stay close.
